en.greeting: Hi! You already understand fast, casual English. Today you start using it yourself: informal words that make you sound relaxed, slang you can (and can't) use, and the British and American words that can save you from an embarrassing moment. Let's start with gonna and wanna.

steps.title: Informal, but still grammatical
steps.text: You understand gonna and wanna at speed. Now let's use them correctly.
steps.body:
**gonna** replaces only *going to*, so the **be** stays: **I'm gonna**, **she's gonna**, **they're gonna**. Indonesian has no *to be* (*aku mau telepon*), so *I gonna call you* is the classic slip: to a native ear it's a mistake, not relaxed English.

**wanna** = *want to*: *I wanna*, but *she **wants to*** (never *she wanna*). **gotta** is the exception: *I gotta go* is normal, because it comes from *I've got to*.

All three are for speech and chats with friends, never emails.

pairs.id: aku bakal / mau (= I'm going to)
kamu mau …? (= Do you want to …?)
aku harus pergi (= I've got to go)

steps.title: Hedges and vague words
steps.text: In casual talk, native speakers rarely sound 100% exact. These small words make you sound relaxed instead of blunt.
steps.body: **kind of / sort of** = agak, semacam · **-ish** = sekitar (*sevenish*, *fortyish*) · **a bit** = agak (British speakers use it for understatement: *a bit annoyed* can mean quite angry) · **or something** = atau semacamnya · **and stuff** = dan lain-lain. Great in chats and conversation; in a report, be precise instead (*at approximately 7 p.m.*).

examples.en: The new office is kind of far from the station.
examples.id: Kantor barunya agak jauh dari stasiun.

examples.en: Let's meet at the café at sevenish.
examples.id: Ketemu di kafe sekitar jam tujuh, ya.

examples.en: I'm a bit tired, to be honest.
examples.id: Jujur, aku agak capek.

examples.en: We could get bakso or something.
examples.id: Kita bisa makan bakso atau apa gitu.

examples.en: We talked about the budget, the deadline and stuff.
examples.id: Kami membahas anggaran, tenggat waktu, dan lain-lain.

steps.title: Build the voice note
steps.text: Rina is driving to a friend's birthday dinner in Bandung, and the traffic on the toll road is terrible. She sends a quick voice note to the group.

question.prompt: Build her message: Kami bakal agak telat.
question.solution: We're gonna be a bit late.
question.explanation: **We're gonna** keeps the *be* ('re = are), just like *we're going to*. **a bit** softens *late*: agak telat. Without the 're (*We gonna be late*) it sounds like a mistake, not like relaxed English.

steps.title: Everyday informal words
steps.text: Some informal words are everywhere in casual English, and some belong more to one country.
steps.body: **reckon** = think (British/Australian; in the US it can sound rural). **fancy** (British) = want: *Fancy a coffee?* Careful: *I fancy him* = aku naksir dia! **cheers** (British) = thanks, bye, or a toast. **mate** (UK/Australia) = friend. **guys** = everyone, women included (*Hi guys!*), but in written work messages *Hi all / Hi everyone* is safer. **no worries** = no problem. **my bad** = my mistake (small ones only). **to be fair** (British) = adds a point on the other side.

steps.title: Chat or email?
steps.text: Rina writes two messages this morning: a WhatsApp to Tom, a friend from her master's course in Leeds, and an email to Mr Clarke, a client in London she has never met.

question.prompt: Which pair is right for each reader?
options: To Tom: 'Wanna grab lunch on Saturday?' · To Mr Clarke: 'Wanna have a quick call tomorrow?'
To Tom: 'Would you be available for lunch on Saturday?' · To Mr Clarke: 'Fancy a quick call tomorrow, mate?'
To Tom: 'Wanna grab lunch on Saturday?' · To Mr Clarke: 'Would you be available for a short call tomorrow?'
question.explanation: **wanna** is perfect in a chat with a friend, but it never goes in an email to a client you've never met: that needs **Would you be available …?** The middle option has it backwards: stiff with a friend, and *Fancy … mate?* is far too casual for a new client.

steps.title: Slang: know it, use it with care
steps.text: Slang is the most informal layer of English. You already know how it works from Indonesian.
steps.body: Think of **bahasa gaul**: *mager*, *gabut* or *anjay* are fine with friends, but you wouldn't tell a director *Maaf, Pak, saya mager*. English slang is the same. Some is common and fairly safe in casual talk (*cool, awesome, broke, a rip-off*); some belongs to younger people or the internet (*sus, lowkey, vibe*) and dates fast; some is offensive, and we don't teach it. Rule: understand lots, use a little. **When in doubt, leave it out.**

pairs.id: 1 dolar (US) · 1 pound (UK): ten bucks, ten quid

steps.title: What happened?
steps.text: Budi had two interviews with a startup in Bandung. They promised him an answer 'next week'. That was two months ago: no email, no call, nothing. He tells a friend: 'Honestly, they totally ghosted me.'

options: They frightened him during the interviews.
They suddenly stopped all contact, with no explanation.
They told him politely that he didn't get the job.
question.explanation: **ghost someone** = stop replying and disappear without explaining (menghilang tanpa kabar). It has nothing to do with being scary, and a polite 'no' is the opposite of ghosting: they would have explained.

steps.title: Safe at work?
steps.text: Sari is posting in her company's Slack channel. The members are her team and the new regional director from Singapore, whom she hasn't met yet. The client has just approved the team's design.

options: Guys!! The client was totally vibing with our design, lowkey obsessed 🔥🔥
Great news, everyone: the client has approved our design. Thanks for all your hard work!
Client approved it. Kinda sus how fast, but whatever lol.
question.explanation: A work channel with a senior person you haven't met calls for neutral English: **Great news, everyone** is warm but professional. *vibing*, *lowkey* and *sus* are youth and internet slang: fine with friends, but at work they can sound unprofessional or like trying too hard, and *whatever lol* sounds as if you don't care.

steps.title: British and American words
steps.text: British and American English share almost everything, but some everyday words differ, and a few can embarrass you.
steps.body: Indonesians already say **lift** and **CV**, like the British; Americans say *elevator* and *résumé*. Understand both, and choose one variety for your own writing. Watch the traps: in the UK **pants** = underwear (celana dalam), so say **trousers**. The UK **first floor** is one level above the street (the *ground floor*): the American *second floor*. In the US a **biscuit** is a soft savoury bread roll, and **football** means American football.

steps.title: A compliment in Manchester
steps.text: Dimas is on a work trip in Manchester. His British colleague James arrives at the office in smart new grey trousers, and Dimas wants to compliment him.

options: Nice pants, James!
Nice trousers, James!
Nice pant, James!
question.explanation: In British English **pants** means underwear (celana dalam), so 'Nice pants!' would get a laugh or an awkward silence. Say **trousers**. In the US, *pants* would be fine. 'pant' is wrong in everyday English: like *jeans*, the word is always plural.

steps.text: Everything on one page.

id.greeting: Hai! Kamu sudah memahami bahasa Inggris yang cepat dan santai. Hari ini kamu mulai memakainya sendiri: kata-kata santai yang membuatmu terdengar rileks, slang yang boleh (dan tidak boleh) kamu pakai, serta kata-kata Inggris dan Amerika yang bisa menyelamatkanmu dari momen memalukan. Kita mulai dari gonna dan wanna.

steps.title: Santai, tapi tetap benar
steps.text: Kamu sudah paham gonna dan wanna dalam ucapan cepat. Sekarang kita pakai dengan benar.
steps.body:
**gonna** hanya menggantikan *going to*, jadi **be**-nya tetap ada: **I'm gonna**, **she's gonna**, **they're gonna**. Bahasa Indonesia tidak punya *to be* (*aku mau telepon*), jadi *I gonna call you* adalah kekeliruan klasik: bagi penutur asli itu salah, bukan santai.

**wanna** = *want to*: *I wanna*, tapi *she **wants to*** (tidak pernah *she wanna*). **gotta** adalah pengecualian: *I gotta go* itu wajar, karena berasal dari *I've got to*.

Ketiganya untuk ucapan dan chat dengan teman, tidak pernah untuk email.

pairs.id: aku bakal / mau (= I'm going to)
kamu mau …? (= Do you want to …?)
aku harus pergi (= I've got to go)

steps.title: Pelunak dan kata-kata samar
steps.text: Dalam obrolan santai, penutur asli jarang terdengar 100% persis. Kata-kata kecil ini membuatmu terdengar rileks, tidak blak-blakan.
steps.body: **kind of / sort of** = agak, semacam · **-ish** = sekitar (*sevenish*, *fortyish*) · **a bit** = agak (orang Inggris memakainya untuk mengecilkan: *a bit annoyed* bisa berarti cukup marah) · **or something** = atau semacamnya · **and stuff** = dan lain-lain. Pas untuk chat dan obrolan; di laporan, tulislah dengan persis (*at approximately 7 p.m.*).

steps.title: Susun pesan suaranya
steps.text: Rina sedang menyetir ke acara makan malam ulang tahun temannya di Bandung, dan jalan tolnya macet parah. Ia mengirim pesan suara singkat ke grup.

question.prompt: Susun pesannya: Kami bakal agak telat.
question.solution: We're gonna be a bit late.
question.explanation: **We're gonna** mempertahankan *be*-nya ('re = are), sama seperti *we're going to*. **a bit** memperlunak *late*: agak telat. Tanpa 're (*We gonna be late*) kalimatnya terdengar salah, bukan santai.

steps.title: Kosakata santai sehari-hari
steps.text: Sebagian kata santai ada di mana-mana dalam bahasa Inggris sehari-hari, dan sebagian lebih milik satu negara.
steps.body: **reckon** = kira (Inggris/Australia; di AS bisa terdengar seperti orang desa). **fancy** (Inggris) = mau: *Fancy a coffee?* Hati-hati: *I fancy him* = aku naksir dia! **cheers** (Inggris) = makasih, dah, atau bersulang. **mate** (Inggris/Australia) = teman. **guys** = semuanya, termasuk perempuan (*Hi guys!*), tapi di pesan tertulis di kantor *Hi all / Hi everyone* lebih aman. **no worries** = nggak masalah. **my bad** = salahku (kesalahan kecil saja). **to be fair** (Inggris) = menambah poin dari sisi lain.

steps.title: Chat atau email?
steps.text: Pagi ini Rina menulis dua pesan: WhatsApp ke Tom, teman kuliah S2-nya di Leeds, dan email ke Mr Clarke, klien di London yang belum pernah ia temui.

question.prompt: Pasangan mana yang tepat untuk masing-masing pembaca?
options: To Tom: 'Wanna grab lunch on Saturday?' · To Mr Clarke: 'Wanna have a quick call tomorrow?'
To Tom: 'Would you be available for lunch on Saturday?' · To Mr Clarke: 'Fancy a quick call tomorrow, mate?'
To Tom: 'Wanna grab lunch on Saturday?' · To Mr Clarke: 'Would you be available for a short call tomorrow?'
question.explanation: **wanna** pas sekali di chat dengan teman, tapi tidak pernah masuk ke email untuk klien yang belum pernah kamu temui: di situ perlu **Would you be available …?** Pilihan tengah terbalik: kaku untuk teman, dan *Fancy … mate?* terlalu santai untuk klien baru.

steps.title: Slang: pahami, lalu pakai dengan hati-hati
steps.text: Slang adalah lapisan paling santai dari bahasa Inggris. Kamu sudah tahu cara kerjanya dari bahasa Indonesia.
steps.body: Ingat **bahasa gaul**: *mager*, *gabut* atau *anjay* tidak masalah dengan teman, tapi kamu tidak akan bilang *Maaf, Pak, saya mager* ke direktur. Slang bahasa Inggris juga begitu. Sebagian umum dan cukup aman di obrolan santai (*cool, awesome, broke, a rip-off*); sebagian milik anak muda atau internet (*sus, lowkey, vibe*) dan cepat basi; sebagian kasar, dan tidak kami ajarkan. Aturannya: pahami banyak, pakai sedikit. **Kalau ragu, jangan dipakai.**

pairs.id: 1 dolar (US) · 1 pound (UK): ten bucks, ten quid

steps.title: Apa yang terjadi?
steps.text: Budi dua kali wawancara di sebuah startup di Bandung. Mereka menjanjikan jawaban 'minggu depan'. Itu dua bulan lalu: tidak ada email, tidak ada telepon, tidak ada apa-apa. Ia bercerita ke temannya: 'Honestly, they totally ghosted me.'

options: They frightened him during the interviews.
They suddenly stopped all contact, with no explanation.
They told him politely that he didn't get the job.
question.explanation: **ghost someone** = berhenti membalas dan menghilang tanpa penjelasan (menghilang tanpa kabar). Tidak ada hubungannya dengan menakut-nakuti, dan penolakan yang sopan justru kebalikan dari ghosting: mereka akan memberi penjelasan.

steps.title: Aman di kantor?
steps.text: Sari menulis di kanal Slack kantornya. Anggotanya adalah timnya dan direktur regional baru dari Singapura yang belum pernah ia temui. Klien baru saja menyetujui desain tim.

options: Guys!! The client was totally vibing with our design, lowkey obsessed 🔥🔥
Great news, everyone: the client has approved our design. Thanks for all your hard work!
Client approved it. Kinda sus how fast, but whatever lol.
question.explanation: Kanal kerja dengan atasan senior yang belum kamu kenal butuh bahasa Inggris netral: **Great news, everyone** hangat tapi profesional. *vibing*, *lowkey* dan *sus* adalah slang anak muda dan internet: tidak masalah dengan teman, tapi di kantor bisa terdengar tidak profesional atau terlalu memaksa, dan *whatever lol* terdengar seolah kamu tidak peduli.

steps.title: Kosakata Inggris dan Amerika
steps.text: Bahasa Inggris versi Inggris dan Amerika hampir sama, tapi beberapa kata sehari-hari berbeda, dan beberapa bisa membuatmu malu.
steps.body: Orang Indonesia sudah bilang **lift** dan **CV**, seperti orang Inggris; orang Amerika bilang *elevator* dan *résumé*. Pahami keduanya, dan pilih satu ragam untuk tulisanmu sendiri. Awas jebakannya: di Inggris **pants** = celana dalam, jadi bilang **trousers**. **First floor** versi Inggris adalah satu lantai di atas level jalan (*ground floor*): *second floor* versi Amerika. Di AS, **biscuit** adalah roti kecil yang lembut dan gurih, dan **football** berarti American football.

steps.title: Pujian di Manchester
steps.text: Dimas sedang dinas ke Manchester. Rekan kerjanya dari Inggris, James, datang ke kantor dengan celana panjang abu-abu baru yang rapi, dan Dimas ingin memujinya.

options: Nice pants, James!
Nice trousers, James!
Nice pant, James!
question.explanation: Dalam bahasa Inggris Inggris **pants** berarti celana dalam, jadi 'Nice pants!' akan membuat orang tertawa atau suasana jadi canggung. Bilang **trousers**. Di AS, *pants* tidak masalah. 'pant' salah dalam bahasa Inggris sehari-hari: seperti *jeans*, katanya selalu jamak.
